title: What's a Tabia? | Grunfeld Theory: Fianchetto System | GM Naroditsky’s Top Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: Whatever your repertoire, you meet the knight to f3 with the very same setup — it so often just transposes back into a queen's-pawn opening anyway.
Black fianchettoes with g6 — the gateway to both the Grünfeld and the King's Indian.
White opts for the Fianchetto System, answering with a quiet g3 of his own.
Black completes the fianchetto, the bishop to g7 raking the long diagonal.
White mirrors it, the bishop out to g2.
Both sides castle, and here is the main crossroads. A King's Indian player reaches for d6 — but as Grünfeld players, we have something sharper in mind.
And there it is, the Grünfeld move d5 — striking in the centre at once rather than building behind it, reaching a symmetrical picture.
White plays the main line c4. This is deep theory, rarely seen at this level, and a welcome gap to fill.
The solid, top-grandmaster choice is a Slav-like c6, but the sharper and more testing try at club level is to grab the pawn — the capture on c4.

White recovers with the knight to a3, the correct move — and now comes an instructive procedure. Black cannot actually keep the extra pawn: clinging to it with the bishop to e6 runs into the knight to g5, and after the bishop to d5, White hits back with e4 and the whole centre falls. The pawn is condemned, so use it to inflict the most damage on White's structure.
So, on Black's own terms: push the pawn to c3, forcing White to capture and accept some structural damage rather than simply handing the pawn back.
White has to take with the b-pawn. Yes, it bolsters the centre — but now the c3-pawn is backward and White is saddled with an isolated a-pawn.

But Black cannot doze, or White prepares e4. So Black counterstrikes at once with the classic Grünfeld break c5, reaching what is called a tabia — a rich standard position with five or six viable continuations, loaded both positionally and tactically. Handle it imprecisely and the knight comes to c6, piling onto d4.
Could Black play c5 before c3? Yes, it is fully playable — though after the recapture the position can drift symmetrical, and Black must be careful not to let that fianchetto bishop spring to life.

A subtle point: it actually suits Black for that knight to stay on f3, since it dampens the fianchetto bishop while Black unwinds the queenside. And here is Grünfeld philosophy in a sentence — activity is sacred. You are ready to give up a pawn as early as move four or five; whatever happens, keep the pieces active, or you may as well be playing the Queen's Gambit Declined.

White lifts the rook to e1 — not the main line, but popular now, preparing e4. Yet e4 is double-edged: it grabs the centre, but it loosens the d4-pawn and lets Black's light bishop come to g4, pressing the knight and so the pawn behind it. Sometimes you want to invite the push, not prevent it.

An instructive slip here would be the bishop to f5 — premature, because it leaves b7 undefended and White has nasty tries like the queen to b3 or the knight jumping to e5. So Black develops soundly instead, the knight to c6.

White plays h3, ruling out the bishop to g4. The next-best home for the light bishop is f5 — it discourages e4 and later eyes e4 itself, to neutralise White's strong bishop. But beware a known trick: after the bishop to f5, White has d5, and if the knight takes, e4 forks the two minor pieces — though even then the c3-pawn hangs and things turn wildly complicated, sometimes three pawns for the piece. It is far from forced. A calmer path is the queen to a5, hitting the knight and the c3-pawn and clearing d8 for a rook.

Black chooses the steadier queen to a5, posing an awkward question: how does White hold the c3-pawn? And notice the tactical undercurrent — the queen now x-rays the rook on e1. If White ever swings the queen to b3, a deflection appears: capture on d4, recapture, and the knight on f3 is dragged away, then take on e1 with check. The check is the point — it buys the time to save the queen. Any move that leaves a rook with only one defender invites exactly this down the diagonal.
Black should also watch the knight on a3 — the bishop to d2 would simply win it. So White's best, perhaps only move, is the bishop to b2. And Black keeps pressing the centre with a familiar tool.

The rook comes to d8. And an instructive doubt creeps in: the queen to a5 may have been a touch inaccurate, because the bishop landing on b2 actually helps White, shoring up the centre and making d4 harder to hit. But Black is in too deep now; the rook to d8 is automatic, and the battle rages over the centre — Black trying to make White's centre collapse, White trying to expand it.
